job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jamal, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in power systems at Harbury, and I still live with my parents because the campus is twenty minutes by bus. A normal day is a lecture on grid stability, then hours in the simulation lab, then home for dinner. My dad is a pharmacist and my mum is a school secretary, so the house is loud and nosy. I did internships at the regional grid operator and at a solar installer, and what I like most is the moment a messy grid model finally balances. What wears me out is applying for things I don't need yet, since the recruiters already email me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, a bit like spreadsheets in the nineties. At the grid operator the engineers used a forecasting tool that saved them about an hour a day, and nobody lost a job. To friends I'd say we'll still need people who understand why the lights stay on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the energy transition makes my field safe whatever AI does. Every country is adding solar, batteries and heat pumps, and somebody has to model that grid. I'd finish the master's, take a graduate offer, and push for a union rep at whatever company I join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on my course and accept a graduate role at the grid operator or a network company next summer. I'd use an AI coding helper now and then for scripting, since I already do. I'd also keep volunteering at the community solar project my mum's school started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My work feels needed and my family can help if something goes wrong, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing, mostly. Even with a good salary, prices where I live make buying a flat feel far away, and my parents would like me to move out eventually. Nothing to do with AI, but it's the thing I'd bring up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for a union rep. Why, if things are fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because things are fine until they aren't, and nobody gets organised after the layoff letter. My uncle was in a factory that closed, and the workers who had a union got a decent package. I'd rather have the structure in place while it's boring.

My real worry is **housing**, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and that the transition from this is going to be bumpy for anyone in a screen job. Among friends from computing, I'd say get your hands on something physical, because software tasks are the first to go. Online I'd write about retraining funds, since I think that's where the argument is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my field splits in two. The modelling, scripting and report writing parts of my job are exactly the thinking tasks the card says get taken over, so juniors may be fewer. But commissioning a substation, tuning protection, dealing with a regulator are slower, so I'd be OK if I get into the physical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the grid operator for a role that mixes field work and modelling, and I'd use AI tools properly for the scripting so I'm the one who can direct them. I'd also sign up for a short course in protection and control, which is more hands-on. And I'd help organise a graduate group at work to talk to management about training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine in myself, but I'm watching friends in pure software get fewer interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your friends would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Tomas, who did computer science and wants a developer job. He's sent sixty applications and heard back from four. His course didn't have the physical side like mine, so he can't pivot easily, and his parents can't support him as long as mine can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're saying you'd lean harder on AI tools. Doesn't that speed up your own juniors being cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the contradiction, I won't pretend otherwise. If I learn to direct a modelling tool, a firm needs fewer people like me. But refusing doesn't save anyone, so my plan is to be the one who understands the physical grid behind the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to be loud, because 2028 is nothing. I'd say governments should talk to unions and universities now, and nobody should be fired before a support plan is in place. I'd put that online even if friends say I'm being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared in a quiet way. If thinking AI is doing almost any desk work by 2028, the graduate market I'm about to enter is gone before I finish my master's. My field does give me the physical side, with robots 3 years behind, but I don't know how many of those jobs will exist when everybody rushes towards them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to finish the master's a term early, then take a hands-on graduate role in the field, like a substation, as soon as I could. I'd use every AI tool I can to stay valuable. And I'd talk with my parents about keeping their savings flexible, because I might need to help them as well as the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not about me starving, it's about nobody knowing what the rules are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your master's if everything is moving that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It becomes a bet. A master's is a year of earning I'd lose, but the knowledge is what makes me useful for the physical, regulated side. If nothing else, it helps me argue for the people who'll be pushed out, and I can write the proposals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk with your parents about savings. What would that conversation be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my dad at the kitchen table and say we should treat his pharmacy income and my mum's job as the stable parts. My dad would say I'm panicking, and I'd say I'm planning. Probably we'd compromise on keeping six months in cash and not buying the flat we talked about.

say: I'd be loud online: **2028** is nothing, and nobody should be fired before a support plan exists.
I'd tell governments to talk to **unions** and universities now.

The physical side of the grid gives me about **3 extra years**, if I'm early.

feel: **Anxious**, but about unclear rules rather than going hungry.

steps.text: Finish the master's a term early and apply to substation roles
Use AI modelling tools daily to stay useful
Agree with my parents to hold six months of cash
Write to my MP asking for a support plan before layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a transition but only if we start. I'd tell friends to pick a path where people matter, like energy, care or construction. And I'd say publicly that a graduate guarantee could be paid for out of the efficiency gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I have a window. 2031 is the date for thinking work, and I'd be 29. In that time I could be at the grid operator, building the kind of experience that makes me hard to replace, and robots for hands-on work wouldn't be fully there until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, join the operator and aim to be the engineer who commissions things in person. I'd study for professional registration, and I'd take a course on AI-based forecasting so I'm not replaced by it. And I'd save about half my salary for the first two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a motivated way. Five years makes me feel like I'm in a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five-year gap make you more or less likely to start a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more cautious. My girlfriend Anjali and I talked about it, and we'd probably marry but delay kids until we see which way things go. It's not fear exactly, it's wanting to know the world a bit more first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anjali if you got laid off in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Anjali that we have savings and that I'd take a site job on any grid project in the country if I had to. And I'd say her work in healthcare is steady, which is a relief. I'd want my girlfriend to hear it from me early, not after I'd been hiding it for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should use it. I'd tell friends to treat it like climate change, which is slow enough to ignore and big enough to wreck us if we do. And I'd tell my union branch to put it on the agenda today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the best case for me. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a decade in energy, maybe leading a small team. I'd feel fairly secure, and I'd have time to make mistakes and learn from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the graduate role, get registered as a chartered engineer by about 2030, and keep studying. I'd try to be early with AI tools, in a steady way, so I'm not behind when it matters. I'd also look at moving into policy or regulation part-time, because that's where people who understand the grid will be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A decade is long enough that I can fix mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one thing that could spoil the calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being sure and then wrong. If I plan for 2036 and it comes in 2029, my relaxed plan fails. That's why I'd keep six months of cash and not stretch myself on a mortgage too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, no question. It pays back over ten years and it keeps my options open for regulation and policy. I'd finish it, maybe not in a rush, but properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one worries me most, because there's no room to fix a mistake and the institutions I'd rely on are slow. What would help is a clear support plan from government, a union at work, and universities telling students honestly what's coming. I'd also want companies to keep a graduate intake even if they could do without it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we owe the people with fewer options than me. I have a pharmacist dad, no debt and a degree in a field that's needed. A lot of people don't, and my answers sound calmer than they should because of that. I'd want whoever reads this to keep it in mind.

headlineQuote: My uncle was in a factory that closed, and the workers who had a union got a decent package.
portrait: Jamal is 24, doing a **master's** in power systems at Harbury and living with his pharmacist father and school-secretary mother.
He is open to change when it's proven, uses **AI tools** now and then, and leans left on unions and public support.
His field is helped by the energy transition, so he stays calm when little changes.
Fast timelines make him anxious about **unclear rules**, not about hunger, since his family cushion is strong.
He plans a physical, hands-on grid role and wants a union in place early.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, since there is no time to fix mistakes.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **government plan**, a union at work, and honest advice from universities.
Companies keeping a **graduate intake** even if they could do without it.
